blocks.content: The bridge network is Docker's default networking mode, a private, internal network on the host that every container connects to unless told otherwise.

Unless you specify a different network mode, every container attaches to a virtual network bridge (named docker0 on Linux) that Docker creates automatically, effectively its own small private network living entirely on your host.

blocks.alt: Every container lands on this bridge by default

blocks.content: 2. Each Container Gets a Private IP
blocks.text: 2. Each Container Gets a Private IP

blocks.content: Joining the bridge network, a container is assigned its own internal IP address (commonly in the 172.17.0.0/16 range), distinct from the host's own IP and from every other container's.

blocks.alt: A private internal IP, assigned automatically

blocks.content: 3. Reaching the Outside World via NAT
blocks.text: 3. Reaching the Outside World via NAT

blocks.content: A container on the bridge network can still reach the internet, outbound traffic is routed through the Docker host itself using network address translation (NAT), the container's private IP is not directly visible to the outside world at all.

blocks.alt: Outbound traffic is translated through the host

blocks.content: The flip side of that same NAT setup: nothing outside the Docker host can reach a container's bridge IP directly, which is exactly why Port Publishing (covered later in this module) exists, to deliberately open a specific path in.

blocks.alt: Isolated from the outside by default, on purpose

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: The bridge network is Docker's default, every container gets its own private internal IP on it unless told otherwise.
Bridge network containers can reach the internet via NAT, but nothing outside the host can reach them without an explicit published port.
